## The big idea

A river running at constant depth is a solved force balance: the component
of gravity along the sloped bed exactly pays the friction bill at the wetted
walls. No pressure gradient assists — the free surface fired that mechanism
in 9.1 — so **elevation is the only currency**, and the truce it buys is
called *uniform flow* at the *normal depth*. Manning's formula prices the
truce, with an openly dimensional constant that Unit 2 taught you to frisk
at the door.

::: {.callout-note}
### The number in charge: the bed slope $S$
A channel's entire budget, in meters of drop per meter of run. Everything a
pipe bought with a pump and a pressure gradient, a channel must buy with
$S$ — which is why canal routes are surveyed to millimeters per kilometer
and why "just make it flow faster" is not an available instruction.
:::

## Gravity vs. friction, in equilibrium

Take a slab of river: cross-section $A$, length $L$, on slope $S$ (small
angles: $S \approx \sin\theta$). Steady and uniform means no acceleration,
so the along-slope weight component balances the wall shear on the wetted
perimeter $P$:

$$\rho g\, A L\, S = \tau_w\, P L
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\tau_w = \rho g\, R_h\, S,
\quad R_h \equiv \frac{A}{P}.$$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Click for why $R_h$ is the star
The balance says shear stress scales with $A/P$: area is what *earns*
(weight pulling the water downhill lives in the volume), perimeter is what
*charges* (friction lives on the wetted walls — the free surface, rubbing
only on air, works nearly for free). $R_h$ is earnings-per-expense. A pipe
running full has $R_h = D/4$; a wide shallow sheet has $R_h \approx y$. The
same quantity quietly unifies the two worlds — Unit 8's $D$ was $4R_h$ all
along.
:::

Turbulent flow over a rough bed relates $\tau_w$ to velocity the way Unit 8
taught ($\tau_w \propto \rho U^2$ at high Re), so $U \propto \sqrt{R_h S}$.
Manning's contribution was the empirical seasoning — a century of channel
data distilled into

$$U = \frac{1}{n}\, R_h^{2/3}\, S^{1/2} \quad \text{(SI units)},$$

with $n$ a roughness coefficient tabulated by eyeball: glass flume 0.010,
finished concrete 0.012, clean earth 0.022, a natural stream with weeds
0.035-and-up.[^n] The formula is honest about its dishonesty: $n$ carries
units (the $1$ out front is $1\ \mathrm{m^{1/3}/s}$, and in US units it
becomes the infamous $1.49$), so this is engineering's workhorse, not
physics' theorem — CT-2-1's lesson, now with a shovel.

[^n]: The toolbox ships the table as `MANNING_N`. The difference between
$n = 0.012$ and $n = 0.022$ is nearly half your velocity — which is why
canal linings are a real budget line, and why maintenance crews mow.

**Normal depth** $y_n$ is the equilibrium itself: for a given $Q$, $S$, $n$,
and shape, it's the depth at which Manning's $Q = \frac{1}{n} A R_h^{2/3}
S^{1/2}$ balances the books ($A$ and $R_h$ both depend on $y$, so the
toolbox solves it numerically: `Channel.normal_depth(Q)`). Deeper than
$y_n$, gravity wins and the flow accelerates and thins; shallower, friction
wins and it decelerates and deepens. Rivers relax toward $y_n$ the way
marbles relax toward the bottom of a bowl.

One more comparison closes the loop with 9.1: is $y_n$ above or below the
*critical* depth $y_c$? If $y_n > y_c$, uniform flow is subcritical and the
slope is called **mild**; if $y_n < y_c$, uniform flow is supercritical —
a **steep** slope. Note the definition is a *relationship*, not an angle:
the same 0.5% grade can be mild for a big river and steep for a thin sheet.
`classify_slope` renders the verdict, and module 9.3 spends it.

::: {.column-margin}
Best-hydraulic-section problems — what shape moves the most water for the
least concrete — are $R_h$ maximization in costume. The semicircle wins;
the half-hexagon trapezoid is its buildable understudy.
:::

## Play with it

A finished-concrete rectangular channel, 3 m wide, carrying $Q$. Slide the
slope and watch normal depth hunt for equilibrium — and watch the mild/steep
verdict flip as $y_n$ crosses $y_c$.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof Q_92 = Inputs.range([1, 20], {value: 6, step: 1, label: "flow Q (m³/s)"})
viewof S_92 = Inputs.range([0.0002, 0.02], {value: 0.002, step: 0.0002, label: "bed slope S (m/m)"})
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - Q_92
#|   - S_92
b = 3.0
Ss = np.logspace(np.log10(2e-4), np.log10(2e-2), 60)
yns = []
for s in Ss:
    ch = Channel(b=b, m=0.0, n=0.012, S=s)
    yns.append(ch.normal_depth(Q_92))
ch = Channel(b=b, m=0.0, n=0.012, S=S_92)
yn = ch.normal_depth(Q_92)
yc = ch.critical_depth(Q_92)
Fr = ch.froude(Q_92, yn)
verdict = "MILD (uniform flow subcritical)" if yn > yc else "STEEP (uniform flow supercritical)"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.6))
ax.plot(Ss, yns, lw=2.5, color='steelblue', label='normal depth y_n(S)')
ax.axhline(yc, color='crimson', lw=2, ls='--', label=f'critical depth y_c = {yc:.2f} m')
ax.plot(S_92, yn, 'o', ms=12, mfc='gold', mec='k', zorder=5)
ax.annotate(f"  y_n = {yn:.2f} m, Fr = {Fr:.2f}\n  {verdict}", (S_92, yn), fontsize=9)
ax.set_xscale('log')
ax.set_xlabel('bed slope S (log scale)'); ax.set_ylabel('depth (m)')
ax.set_title("steeper slope, thinner faster river — until y_n dives under y_c")
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Three experiments. **Sweep the slope** at fixed $Q$: normal depth falls
monotonically — the same water, moving faster, needs less of itself. **Find
the critical slope**, where the blue curve crosses the red dashed line:
that's the grade at which this channel's uniform flow arrives exactly at
$Fr = 1$ (and where flumes get twitchy — designers avoid loitering near it).
**Crank $Q$** and watch both depths rise but the crossing *move*: mild vs.
steep really is a relationship between flow and geometry, not a property of
the ground.

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
"Wider is bigger, and bigger carries more." Not per unit of concrete. Spread
a given area wide and shallow and you've maximized the wetted perimeter —
all bill, little benefit — while a compact section shelters its area behind
the least possible wall. $R_h = A/P$ is the honest metric; the free surface
is the only boundary that works for free, and good design exploits exactly
that.
:::


Gravity's slope pays friction's perimeter, and Manning is the exchange rate — with the units flag flying openly.

:::

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** A survey error flattens your canal's slope from 0.0020 to 0.0010. By what factor does capacity drop at fixed depth — and what does the channel actually do at fixed $Q$ instead?</summary>
Manning: $Q \propto \sqrt{S}$, so capacity falls to $\sqrt{1/2} \approx
71\%$ at the same depth. Held at the same $Q$, the channel instead deepens
to a new, larger $y_n$ — which is why surveying errors surface as water
climbing the freeboard, not as a polite flow reduction.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** Your 3 m flume runs $y_n = 0.87$ m where $y_c = 0.74$ m. Classify the slope, and predict what a pebble's ripple rings do.</summary>
$y_n > y_c$: mild slope, uniform flow subcritical ($Fr < 1$). Rings make
headway upstream. (The toolbox: `ch.classify_slope(Q)` — but the two
depths already told you.)
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** Why does dredging weeds ($n$: 0.035 → 0.025) lower flood risk even though it doesn't touch the channel's size?</summary>
At fixed $Q$, less roughness means a smaller $y_n$ — the same flood flows
*lower* in the channel. Capacity at the brim rises by the ratio
$0.035/0.025 = 1.4$. Maintenance is hydraulics; the mowing crew is moving
the rating curve.
</details>
